q: An auditor sends positive confirmations for trade receivables. The primary assertion addressed is:
o: Existence of the balance and rights over the receivable
Valuation of the expected credit loss allowance recorded
Classification between current and non-current balances
Completeness of the receivables recorded in the ledger
why: External confirmation of a recorded balance corroborates that the debtor exists and acknowledges the amount, addressing existence and rights. Completeness is poorly served because unrecorded receivables would never be selected for confirmation.

q: A debtor does not respond to a positive confirmation after two follow ups. Under SA 505, the most appropriate alternative procedure is:
o: Send a negative confirmation and treat silence as agreement
Examine subsequent receipts, despatch documents and invoices
Obtain a written representation from management on the balance
Reduce the sample size and select a different debtor instead
why: SA 505 requires alternative procedures such as inspecting subsequent receipts, despatch documentation and invoices to obtain relevant reliable evidence. Substituting a negative confirmation or a management representation does not compensate for a non-response.

q: Negative confirmations may be used as the sole substantive procedure only when all of the following conditions are met EXCEPT:
o: The population has many small homogeneous account balances
A very low exception rate is expected in the population
The debtors are related parties under common control
Risk is assessed as low and the controls operate effectively
why: SA 505 permits sole reliance on negative confirmations where risk is low, the population consists of numerous small homogeneous balances, a low exception rate is expected and there is no reason to expect recipients to disregard requests. Related party status increases risk and makes negative confirmations inappropriate.

q: A material receivable from a related party has been outstanding for 400 days with no repayment. Management asserts no credit loss because the group will support it. The auditor should:
o: Require a 100 percent provision on every related party balance held
Confirm the balance and conclude if the confirmation agrees
Accept the assertion, as the group has always paid in the past
Obtain evidence of the ability and intention of the group to pay
why: A confirmation from a related party corroborates the amount but not recoverability, so evidence of the ability and intention to pay is essential alongside ECL measurement. Companies Act provisions on loans and related party transactions also require evaluation for such balances.

q: Under Ind AS 109, the simplified approach for trade receivables without a significant financing component requires:
o: Lifetime expected credit losses recognised from the start
Losses recognised only when the balance is 90 days overdue
Incurred loss measurement on objective evidence of default
Twelve month expected credit losses at initial recognition
why: The simplified approach requires a loss allowance measured at lifetime expected credit losses from initial recognition, without staging assessments. The 90 day trigger and incurred loss model reflect the superseded approach.

q: Testing subsequent receipts to support the year end receivable balance is weakest as evidence when:
o: The receipt comes soon after year end from an outside customer
The customer pays a lump sum on account, with no allocation
The payment is traced to the bank statement and sales ledger
The customer pays the exact amount of a pre year end invoice
why: An unallocated lump sum on account cannot be matched to the specific year end invoices, so it does not confirm that those particular invoices were valid and outstanding. Invoice specific remittance advices provide much stronger linkage.

q: An auditor is concerned that revenue was recognised for goods despatched after year end. The most direct procedure is:
o: Ageing the receivables ledger by the date of the sales invoice
Reconciling the receivables ledger to the control account
Matching invoices around the cut-off to despatch documents
Circularising the ten largest customers by closing balance
why: Two way matching of despatch documentation to invoices around the cut-off date directly tests whether the transfer of control occurred before or after year end. Ageing and ledger reconciliations do not test the timing of despatch.

q: Management refuses to allow the auditor to send confirmations to three large debtors, citing an ongoing commercial negotiation. Under SA 505, the auditor should first:
o: Send the confirmations anyway without informing the management
Accept the refusal and perform alternative procedures at once
Issue a qualified opinion immediately for a scope limitation
Inquire into the reasons and seek evidence of their validity
why: SA 505 requires inquiry into the reasons for refusal and evidence of their validity, evaluation of the implications for risk including fraud, and performance of alternative procedures. Only if the refusal is unreasonable or alternative procedures fail does the auditor communicate with those charged with governance and consider the opinion implications.

q: A confirmation reply is received by fax from a debtor and shows agreement with the recorded balance. Under SA 505 the auditor should:
o: Consider the reliability risk and verify the source directly
Treat it as an oral response that requires no further follow up
Accept it without further work because the balance agrees
Reject it outright, as only original signed letters count
why: SA 505 recognises that responses received electronically or by fax carry risks about source and authorisation, so the auditor takes steps to validate the source and integrity. Outright rejection is not required, but unquestioning acceptance is inappropriate.

q: An ageing analysis shows a significant balance in the 0 to 30 day bucket for a customer who historically pays in 120 days. Investigation reveals the old invoices were credited and re-invoiced. This most likely indicates:
o: A legitimate correction of pricing errors on old invoices
Ledger churning to disguise the true age of a doubtful debt
A change in the credit terms approved by the board of directors
A genuine improvement in the collection performance this year
why: Cancelling and reissuing invoices resets the ageing clock and hides the true age, understating the expected credit loss. Genuine pricing corrections would normally alter the amount rather than the whole invoice date profile for a slow payer.

q: The auditor tests credit notes issued after the year end. The primary purpose is to:
o: Verify the accuracy of the discount rate used in the ECL model
Confirm the existence of the customer named on the invoice
Identify revenue and receivables to be reversed at year end
Test the completeness of purchases recorded near the year end
why: Post year end credit notes relating to pre year end sales indicate that revenue and receivables were overstated at the balance sheet date. This is a cut-off and valuation procedure rather than an existence one.

q: When designing a positive confirmation, requesting the debtor to provide the amount they believe is owed rather than confirming a stated amount:
o: It raises the response rate and the reliability in equal measure
It is prohibited under SA 505 for trade receivable balances
It is used only in the design of negative confirmations
It lowers the response rate but improves reliability of replies
why: A blank form positive confirmation avoids the respondent simply signing an agreed figure, so the responses received are more reliable, but the extra effort typically lowers response rates. SA 505 permits both blank and stated amount forms.

q: Which procedure best addresses the completeness assertion for trade receivables?
o: Tracing despatches before year end into invoices and the ledger
Reviewing the ageing report for the oldest outstanding balances
Recalculating the expected credit loss allowance at the year end
Confirming a sample of balances drawn from the sales ledger
why: Tracing from despatch documentation forward to invoices and the ledger detects unrecorded sales, which is the essence of completeness. Confirmation and ageing both start from recorded balances and cannot reveal omissions.

q: A debtor confirmation reply states that the amount was paid on 28 March, but the company records show the receipt on 4 April. This exception most likely reflects:
o: A misstatement needing adjustment of the receivable balance
Cash in transit, to be traced to the bank reconciliation
Evidence of a ghost customer created to inflate the revenue
A breach of the simplified approach under Ind AS 109 rules
why: Cash in transit at the cut-off is a routine reconciling item that must be traced to the bank statement and the reconciliation to confirm it is genuine. It becomes a misstatement only if the receipt cannot be substantiated or was deliberately delayed.

q: For a bill discounted with a bank with recourse, the correct treatment and audit focus is:
o: Net the discounted bills off against the trade payables
Derecognise the receivable, as the risk has passed to the bank
Keep the receivable, record the borrowing and test recourse
Disclose it only as a contingent liability in the notes
why: Where the entity retains substantially all risks and rewards through recourse, derecognition criteria under Ind AS 109 are not met, so the receivable stays on the books with a corresponding liability. Treating it as an off balance sheet contingency understates both assets and borrowings.

q: An auditor selects confirmations only from balances above Rs 25 lakh in a ledger where numerous smaller balances aggregate to a material amount. The main deficiency is:
o: Positive confirmations may not be used for large balances
Sampling is not permitted for trade receivable balances
It breaches a requirement to confirm every open balance
The untested stratum may hold material aggregate error
why: Selecting only large items leaves the remaining population untested, and those balances can aggregate to a material misstatement. The auditor must apply sampling or other substantive procedures to the residual stratum.

q: Control of confirmation requests under SA 505 requires that:
o: The auditor selects, sends and receives the replies directly
Replies may be routed via the client accounts team for sorting
Management may decide which non-responses need to be chased
The client posts the requests while the auditor reviews the list
why: SA 505 requires the auditor to maintain control over the entire confirmation process, including sending requests and receiving replies directly. Client involvement in mailing or receiving replies destroys the independence that gives confirmations their evidential value.

q: A company sells receivables without recourse to a factor at a discount, transferring substantially all risks and rewards. At year end the auditor should verify that:
o: The receivables stay on the balance sheet with a factoring loan
The receivables are derecognised and the loss is recognised
The factoring discount is capitalised as a prepaid expense
The arrangement is disclosed only in the directors report
why: Where substantially all risks and rewards transfer, Ind AS 109 requires derecognition with the difference recognised in profit or loss. Retaining the asset would be correct only for recourse arrangements where risks are retained.
